Subject: Spike absorption and autoscale guardrails for Elara

Hi Avery / Ben / Monica,

Thanks again for the demo last week — excited about what Redwood can do for our inference costs. We're planning a marketing-driven product surge in Q3 (two 4-week peaks) and need a Dedicated setup that can absorb short spikes without breaking SLAs. High level:

- Baseline expected steady usage: ~450 concurrent sessions (avg. 1.2k tokens per session).
- Peak spikes observed historically: up to ~3.5x baseline for short windows (1–3 hours), occasional 6x micro-spikes for <15 minutes.
- Latency target: p95 < 250ms for our critical endpoints.

Can you propose a Dedicated sizing + autoscale guardrail that:
- provides predictable monthly cost for baseline capacity,
- supports short-term burst capacity for marketing spikes with clear preemption behavior,
- defines cooldowns, headroom multipliers, and eviction policies so our engineering team can design safe retries,
- includes a fallback plan (hosted or cross-region) if we exhaust Dedicated headroom.

Attaching our current capacity matrix for reference (token-length distributions, qps traces). We're particularly sensitive to preemption during live experiments; some jobs are short-lived and can tolerate preemption, others (batch re-ranks) cannot. Also please call out GPU-family tradeoffs (A100 vs H100) and quantization implications for throughput.

Would love a short proposal by next Tuesday (6/22) so we can feed it into procurement.

Thanks,
Maya
Maya Singh
Head of Platform
Elara Labs

Subject: Re: Spike absorption and autoscale guardrails for Elara

Maya — thanks for the detail and the matrix. High level response below; attached is a short draft of an autoscale guardrail we can iterate on.

Summary proposal (preview):
- Baseline: reserve capacity to cover ~1.5x steady usage (safety slab) to keep cost predictable.
- Spike absorption buffer: provide an ephemeral burst pool sized at +40% of baseline for marketing windows (fast ramp), with the ability to expand to +100% as a short-duration emergency buffer.
- Headroom multiplier: default 1.4 during business hours of the campaign; allow on-demand uplift to 2.0 for pre-authorized campaign windows.
- Eviction & preemption policy: classify workloads as "preemptible-friendly" (stateless inference) vs "pin-needed" (long re-ranks). Preemptible-friendly workloads are eligible for immediate eviction with a 30s notice and credits proportional to token consumption during preemption. Pin-needed workloads require at-rest reservation or routed to the Dedicated baseline.
- Cooldown & smoothing: enforce a 10-minute cooldown after scale-up to prevent oscillation; use continuous batching smoothing to blend micro-spikes.
- Fallback: automatic graceful reroute to Redwood hosted API when Dedicated headroom is fully consumed; add rate-limiting thresholds to protect customer SLAs.

GPU & quantization notes (short):
- H100s provide ~20–30% better latency for long-context workloads; A100 is cost-effective for 8k/16k contexts when quantized.
- Recommend mixed pool: H100 for pin-needed low-latency endpoints, A100+int8 quantized paths for high-throughput stateless calls.

Next steps:
1) We run a 48h synthetic replay using your traces to validate the proposed +40% buffer and simulate preemption impact (we'll need a short access token/trace subset).
2) We finalize an SLA addendum and an autoscale runbook (we'll send a DocuSign SOW for the dedicated uplift).
3) Pilot: 6-week pilot across one campaign window; tune headroom multipliers post-pilot.

I've attached a short PDF with the draft autoscale policy and example runbook items. If this looks reasonable, Monica and I can put a pricing sketch together for procurement.

Quick tech notes before we send the replay job:

- For the synthetic replay, we'll generate two profiles: campaign-ramp (gradual 3.5x for 2 hours) and micro-spike (6x for up to 15 minutes). Use token distribution from sheet col C/D.
- Kernel/runtime: prefer H100 for campaign-ramp samples where p95 matters; A100 with int8 paths for micro-spike throughput tests (cheaper and hits higher throughput).
- KV-cache behavior: ensure we run the replay with cold and warm cache states; warm cache reduces tokens-per-request cost but increases memory pressure (affects eviction).

I'll set up the replay cluster on our lab fleet and share the replay job id here.
